summary: A belated record of a 1979 BBN meeting about the state of computer mail in the ARPA community. It tried to guide development of mail systems so they would still form a coherent total service.

plainLanguage.summary: Three years late, someone wrote up notes from a meeting about email so everyone could follow the same plan.

subtitle: Summary of a 1979 meeting on unifying the chaotic state of ARPANET email.

tldr.problem: By 1979, dozens of incompatible email systems had been built across the ARPANET, each with variations that broke other systems and threatened the coherence of email as a network service.
tldr.mechanism: Representatives from major ARPA sites met to understand the problems, agree on freezing the current text mail service, and commit to building a next-generation system supporting multimedia.
tldr.outcome: The meeting produced rules to stabilize text mail (no spaces in usernames, no multiple @ signs) and a decision to focus future work on structured multimedia mail protocols rather than patching the existing system.

today: RFC 808 is a historical snapshot of email in crisis. The problems it describes—incompatible variants, lack of standards, and lack of structure—plagued email until SMTP, RFC 822, and especially MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provided real solutions. The meeting's decision to freeze text mail and build multimedia mail from scratch led to RFC 759 and RFC 767, which were the intellectual foundations for modern MIME-based email.

sections.title: The Problem: Incompatible Mail Systems
sections.content:
This document, written in 1982, records a meeting held at BBN in Cambridge, Massachusetts on 10 January 1979. At that time, email was supposed to be a unified service across the ARPANET, but it had become fractured. Each site had built its own mail system—there was SNDMSG, READMAIL, MSG, HERMES, HG, MAIL, COMSAT, BABYL, and dozens more, each on different computers running TENEX, TOPS-10, TOPS-20, UNIX, Multics, or IBM systems.

The problem was that these systems were not fully compatible. Minor changes in one system would unexpectedly break other systems. For example, variations in how mail addresses were written, how FTP servers responded, and how host tables were maintained were causing service failures across the network. The RFC notes that the text mail service was somewhat out of control with incompatible variations and extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer had its own email program, and they didn't agree on how email should work. When one place changed something, it would break email at other places.

sections.title: What Was Breaking Email
sections.content:
The problems were both technical and procedural. Technically, the RFC 733 protocol allowed features that most implementations did not support—features like "Include" and "Postal" type addresses. Since most systems did not implement these, adding them broke compatibility. Other issues included:

  • Spaces in usernames caused delivery failures
  • Multiple @ signs in mailbox addresses created ambiguity
  • Strange FTP server replies (e.g., "System going down in 10 minutes") were misinterpreted as mail delivery errors
  • Host table update problems led to mail bouncing

The meeting also heard complaints about missing features people wanted: authentication, message identification, duplicate detection, prevention of email spoofing, multicopy delivery with limits, program-to-program mail, and support for graphics, fax, and voice.

One speaker summed it up bluntly: further work on the current system was just putting patches on patches. A commitment to a version 2 system was needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules in RFC 733 allowed things that nobody actually used, which confused people. Some formats didn't work across systems. Everyone wanted different new features added, but adding them broke things.

sections.title: The Stabilization Strategy
sections.content:
The meeting concluded that the existing text mail service had to be frozen. No more changes would be made except for a few minor refinements. Duane Adams from ARPA would arbitrate any disputes about whether a change was permitted.

The specific rules were:

  • Spaces in usernames and multiple @ signs are forbidden—mail shall not be sent between hosts if it breaks existing mail programs.
  • Unimplemented RFC 733 features are decommitted—features like "Include" and "Postal" type addresses would remain permanently unimplemented and were no longer part of the specification.
  • No more changes to MAIL/MLFL FTP reply codes—this had been a source of confusion.

The philosophy was pragmatic: stabilize the service in a useful state by preventing incompatible changes, rather than trying to complete the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: They decided: no more changes to the basic email system. If a change breaks other systems, don't do it. The leader at ARPA would decide any arguments about what's allowed.

sections.title: The Future Direction
sections.content:
Rather than trying to patch the existing system, the meeting's key decision was to shift focus to a new, structured multimedia mail architecture. New services should be provided in the context of experimental multimedia mail systems, not in the existing text mail framework.

Jack Haverty noted that RFC 713 had specified a language called MSDTP that could define a structured mail protocol. The consensus was that future email should use structured data (typed message components) rather than the plain text approaches that were causing compatibility problems.

The group also assigned action items: Jon Postel would draft a specification of a structured mail protocol, and everyone would submit position papers on addressing and system architecture. These became the foundation for RFC 759 and RFC 767, which defined multimedia mail structures.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of trying to fix the old email, they decided to design something completely new that could handle pictures, voice, and text all organized in a clear structure.

sections.title: The Role of Personal Computers and New Services
sections.content:
The meeting anticipated challenges that would become central to email design for decades. Personal computers were starting to exist, but they would not run all the time. The solution: personal computer users would keep their mailboxes on a larger host computer and poll for mail when they wanted to read it. This is the principle behind POP (Post Office Protocol), developed years later.

Bob Thomas from BBN proposed treating an entire user community (like the NSW—Network Standard Workstations) as a virtual host. Rather than addressing mail to a specific machine, you would address it to the user within the virtual community. The system would then route it appropriately. This idea of virtual addressing remains fundamental to modern email.

The meeting also acknowledged that as mail services became more sophisticated, they needed to ensure compatibility with emerging standards from ANSI X3 S33, IFIP TC 6.5 (international message services), and the US Congress Office of Technology Assessment.
sections.plainLanguage: They realized computers wouldn't always be on, so people should check their mail on a central server. Also, email addresses shouldn't be tied to one specific computer—a person should have an address that works no matter where their computer is.
